theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: Device Families, Ratings and Data Sheets
Semiconductor devices can be classified in several independent ways, and a question may use any of them:
items: By number of junctions or layers: one pn junction (diode), two junctions (BJT), three junctions in a pnpn stack (SCR or thyristor), no junction in the current path (the MOSFET channel, the Schottky metal-semiconductor contact).

By carriers: bipolar or minority-carrier devices (pn diode, BJT, SCR) rely on both electrons and holes; unipolar or majority-carrier devices (JFET, MOSFET, Schottky diode) use only one type, so they store almost no charge and switch faster.
By control: two-terminal devices have no control input; the BJT is current-controlled; JFETs, MOSFETs and IGBTs are voltage-controlled.
By power level: small-signal devices (milliwatts, used in amplifiers and logic) versus power devices (watts to kilowatts, used in converters and motor drives), which need heat sinks.

rows: V_BE falls, so current can run away
High g_m, low V_CE(sat) at small currents
Fast switching, easy drive, dense ICs

theoryAdd.text: A data sheet has two distinct parts. The absolute maximum ratings are limits that must never be exceeded, even briefly; operating a device at them gives no safety margin. The electrical characteristics are measured values (minimum, typical, maximum) at stated test conditions, such as h_FE at a given I_C and V_CE. Power ratings are normally quoted at 25 °C, and above that temperature the permissible dissipation is derated linearly: P_D(T) = P_D(25 °C) − k(T − 25), where the derating factor k (in W/°C, often quoted in mW/°C) equals 1/θ_JA, so that P_D(25 °C) = (T_J(max) − 25)/θ_JA.

rows: V_RRM (peak inverse voltage), I_F(AV), I_FSM surge
V_F at rated current, I_R leakage, t_rr
V_Z at test current, dynamic resistance r_z
V_DS(max), V_GS(max) about ±20 V, I_D, P_D
R_DS(on), V_GS(th), gate charge Q_g, capacitances
V_F at rated I_F, luminous intensity, wavelength

theoryAdd.plainText: TJ = TA + PD x (theta_JC + theta_CS + theta_SA)

theoryAdd.text:
Worked example 1: choosing a heat sink
Given: P_D = 15 W, T_J(max) = 150 °C, T_A = 45 °C
       theta_JC = 1.2 °C/W, theta_CS = 0.3 °C/W
Step 1: total theta allowed = (150 - 45) / 15 = 7.0 °C/W
Step 2: theta_SA <= 7.0 - 1.2 - 0.3 = 5.5 °C/W
Step 3: pick a 4.5 °C/W heat sink (below the limit)
Check : T_J = 45 + 15 x (1.2 + 0.3 + 4.5) = 45 + 90 = 135 °C
Result: 135 °C < 150 °C, so the design is safe

theoryAdd.latex: P_{BJT} = V_{CE(sat)} I_C + V_{BE(sat)} I_B, \quad P_{MOS} = I_D^2 R_{DS(on)}
theoryAdd.plainText: P_BJT = VCE(sat) x IC + VBE(sat) x IB;   P_MOS = ID^2 x RDS(on)

theoryAdd.text:
Worked example 2: BJT or MOSFET as a 10 A switch?
BJT   : V_CE(sat) = 0.4 V, forced beta = 10 -> I_B = 1 A, V_BE(sat) = 1.0 V
        P = 0.4 x 10 + 1.0 x 1 = 4 + 1 = 5 W
MOSFET: R_DS(on) = 0.015 ohm, gate current negligible
        P = 10^2 x 0.015 = 1.5 W
Break-even (collector loss only): I^2 x 0.015 = 0.4 x I
        I = 0.4 / 0.015 = 26.7 A
Below about 27 A the MOSFET has the lower conduction loss;
the MOSFET loss grows as I^2, the BJT loss roughly as I.
Common mistakes with ratings and device comparisons:
items: Using the 25 °C power rating at a higher ambient temperature without derating it first.
Adding only the heat-sink thermal resistance and forgetting θ_JC and θ_CS, which are always in series with it.
Assuming V_CEO equals V_CBO; with the base open the collector leakage is multiplied by β, so V_CEO is lower.
Designing for the typical h_FE; a robust bias circuit must work over the full minimum-to-maximum spread.
Treating a MOSFET as lossless when on; R_DS(on) roughly doubles between 25 °C and 150 °C.

theoryAdd.text: A MOSFET gate oxide is only tens of nanometres thick and is destroyed if V_GS exceeds its rating (typically about ±20 V). Static charge from handling easily reaches thousands of volts, so MOSFETs and CMOS ICs are stored in conductive packaging and handled with earthing straps.

For thermal problems write one line: T_J = T_A + P × (sum of all thermal resistances in the path). For derating, subtract k × (T − 25) from the 25 °C rating. For switch losses, BJT loss is V_CE(sat) × I_C (plus base drive) and MOSFET loss is I² × R_DS(on).

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a unipolar device, in which current is carried by only one type of charge carrier?
questions.explanation: In a FET the channel current is carried only by majority carriers (electrons in an n-channel device, holes in a p-channel device). BJTs, pn diodes and SCRs all depend on both electrons and holes crossing junctions.

questions.questionText: A small-signal transistor is rated P_D = 625 mW at 25 °C ambient and is derated linearly at 5 mW/°C above 25 °C. Its maximum permissible dissipation at 75 °C ambient is:
questions.explanation: P_D(75 °C) = 625 − 5 × (75 − 25) = 625 − 250 = 375 mW. Subtracting 5 × 75 instead of 5 × 50 gives the wrong 250 mW.

questions.questionText: A four-layer pnpn device with three junctions, used for controlled rectification, is the:
questions.explanation: The SCR is a pnpn structure with three junctions; a gate pulse latches it on. A BJT has three layers and two junctions, and a Zener diode has one junction.

questions.questionText: A device with a junction-to-ambient thermal resistance θ_JA = 200 °C/W dissipates 0.4 W in an ambient of 30 °C. Its junction temperature is:
questions.explanation: T_J = T_A + P θ_JA = 30 + 0.4 × 200 = 30 + 80 = 110 °C. The 80 °C figure is only the temperature rise, before adding the ambient.

questions.questionText: Among the following, which device offers the highest DC input resistance at its control terminal?
questions.explanation: The oxide-insulated MOSFET gate has an input resistance of 10^12 Ω or more. A JFET gate is a reverse-biased junction, about 10^9 Ω; a BJT input is only kilohms (CE) or tens of ohms (CB).

questions.questionText: Thermal runaway is a failure mechanism mainly associated with:
options: MOSFETs, because their R_DS(on) falls sharply as they heat up
Metal-film resistors, because their resistance rises with temperature
Bipolar junction transistors, because rising temperature increases collector current, which raises the temperature further
questions.explanation: In a BJT, heating lowers V_BE and raises leakage and β, so collector current and dissipation increase, which heats the junction further. A MOSFET's R_DS(on) rises with temperature, which opposes runaway.

questions.questionText: A power transistor has T_J(max) = 150 °C, θ_JC = 1.5 °C/W, case-to-sink θ_CS = 0.5 °C/W and heat-sink θ_SA = 3 °C/W. At an ambient of 40 °C, the maximum power it can dissipate continuously is:
questions.explanation: Total θ = 1.5 + 0.5 + 3 = 5 °C/W, so P = (150 − 40)/5 = 110/5 = 22 W. Using θ_JC alone gives 73.3 W and ignoring the ambient gives 30 W.

questions.questionText: Power MOSFETs can be connected in parallel to share a large current more easily than BJTs because:
options: Their threshold voltages are exactly identical from device to device
R_DS(on) increases with temperature, so a hotter device automatically takes less current
Their gates draw large currents that balance the devices
They have a negative temperature coefficient of on-state resistance
questions.explanation: A MOSFET that carries more current heats up, its R_DS(on) rises and current shifts to the cooler devices, so sharing is self-correcting. BJTs have the opposite tendency, so they need emitter ballast resistors.

questions.questionText: A device dissipates 10 W with T_J(max) = 125 °C at an ambient of 25 °C. Given θ_JC = 2 °C/W and θ_CS = 1 °C/W, the largest heat-sink thermal resistance θ_SA that may be used is:
questions.explanation: Total allowed θ = (125 − 25)/10 = 10 °C/W; θ_SA = 10 − 2 − 1 = 7 °C/W. Forgetting θ_CS gives 8 °C/W and forgetting θ_JC gives 9 °C/W.

questions.questionText: A Schottky diode switches faster than an ordinary pn-junction diode mainly because:
options: It is a majority-carrier device, so almost no minority charge is stored that must be removed at turn-off
It has a larger band gap than silicon
Its forward drop is higher, about 1.5 V
It is always made from germanium
questions.explanation: A metal-semiconductor junction conducts by majority carriers, so there is practically no stored minority charge and hence negligible reverse-recovery time. Its forward drop is lower (about 0.2 to 0.4 V), not higher.

questions.questionText: A MOSFET switch with R_DS(on) = 0.05 Ω carries a steady drain current of 10 A. Its conduction loss is:
questions.explanation: P = I² R_DS(on) = 10² × 0.05 = 5 W. Multiplying I × R gives the voltage drop, 0.5 V, not the power.

questions.questionText: Which statement comparing a BJT with a MOSFET is NOT correct?
options: A MOSFET is a majority-carrier device, whereas a BJT uses both carrier types
At the same bias current, a BJT usually has a higher transconductance than a MOSFET
A BJT has a higher input impedance than a MOSFET
A MOSFET gate draws practically no DC current
questions.explanation: The MOSFET, with its insulated gate, has by far the higher input impedance; the BJT base draws real current. The other three statements are correct.

questions.questionText: A load current of 5 A is switched either by a BJT (V_CE(sat) = 0.3 V, needing I_B = 0.25 A at V_BE(sat) = 0.9 V) or by a MOSFET (R_DS(on) = 0.02 Ω, negligible gate current). By how much does the BJT's total on-state loss (collector plus base) exceed the MOSFET's?
questions.explanation: BJT: 0.3 × 5 + 0.9 × 0.25 = 1.5 + 0.225 = 1.725 W. MOSFET: 5² × 0.02 = 0.5 W. Difference = 1.725 − 0.5 = 1.225 W (ignoring the base drive gives 1.0 W).

questions.questionText: On a rectifier diode data sheet, the rating V_RRM denotes the:
options: Maximum repetitive peak reverse voltage the diode can withstand
Forward voltage drop at rated current
questions.explanation: V_RRM is the repetitive peak reverse voltage, the data-sheet form of the peak inverse voltage (PIV) rating. Forward drop is V_F, recovery time is t_rr and surge current is I_FSM.

questions.questionText: A rectifier diode in a half-wave circuit is fed directly from a 230 V (rms) sinusoidal supply. Allowing a safety factor of 1.5 on the peak inverse voltage, the minimum V_RRM rating to select is about:
questions.explanation: Peak inverse voltage = V_m = 230√2 = 325 V; with the safety factor 1.5 × 325 = 488 V. Forgetting √2 gives 345 V; using 2V_m (centre-tapped full-wave) gives 976 V.

questions.questionText: For a given BJT, how does the collector-emitter breakdown rating V_CEO (base open) compare with the collector-base rating V_CBO (emitter open)?
options: V_CEO is zero because the base is open
questions.explanation: With the base open, the collector-base leakage acts as base current and is multiplied by β, so avalanche breakdown sets in at a lower voltage. Data sheets therefore always show V_CEO below V_CBO.

questions.questionText: A BJT data sheet quotes a transition frequency f_T = 300 MHz and a low-frequency β of 150. The β cut-off frequency f_β, at which β has fallen by 3 dB, is about:
questions.explanation: f_T ≈ β₀ f_β, so f_β = f_T/β₀ = 300 MHz/150 = 2 MHz. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 45 GHz.

questions.questionText: The 'absolute maximum ratings' listed on a transistor data sheet are best described as:
options: Typical values at which the device should normally be operated
Limits that must never be exceeded, even momentarily; they are not recommended operating conditions
Values measured at the point of highest efficiency
questions.explanation: Absolute maximum ratings are stress limits beyond which damage may occur; a good design keeps well inside them. Typical and guaranteed performance figures appear separately under electrical characteristics.

questions.questionText: A BJT has f_T = 300 MHz and a low-frequency β of 150. At a signal frequency of 10 MHz, well above its β cut-off, the magnitude of its common-emitter current gain is approximately:
questions.explanation: Above f_β the gain falls in inverse proportion to frequency, |β| ≈ f_T/f = 300/10 = 30. (The exact value 150/√(1 + 5²) = 29.4 confirms this.)

questions.questionText: Which pairing of a device with its principal application is INCORRECT?
questions.explanation: A photodiode detects light: it is reverse-biased and its current rises with illumination. Light emission is the job of an LED. The other three pairings are correct.

questions.questionText: At a bias current of 1 mA, a BJT (V_T = 26 mV) is compared with a MOSFET in saturation that follows the square law and operates at an overdrive voltage V_GS − V_th = 0.2 V. The ratio g_m(BJT)/g_m(MOSFET) is about:
questions.explanation: BJT: g_m = I_C/V_T = 1 mA/26 mV = 38.5 mA/V. MOSFET: g_m = 2I_D/(V_GS − V_th) = 2 × 1/0.2 = 10 mA/V. Ratio = 38.5/10 = 3.85 (dropping the factor 2 gives 7.7).

questions.questionText: The transition frequency f_T quoted on a BJT data sheet is the frequency at which:
options: The common-base gain α falls to 0.707 of its low-frequency value
The common-emitter short-circuit current gain falls to 1
The voltage gain of any amplifier falls by 3 dB
questions.explanation: f_T is the unity-gain frequency of the short-circuit CE current gain, and f_T ≈ β₀ f_β. The frequency at which α falls by 3 dB is a different figure, f_α.

questions.questionText: A red LED has V_F = 2 V at its rated forward current I_F = 15 mA. The series resistor needed to run it at rated current from a 5 V supply is:
questions.explanation: R = (V_S − V_F)/I_F = (5 − 2)/0.015 = 200 Ω. Ignoring V_F gives 333 Ω; using V_F alone gives 133 Ω.

questions.questionText: On a power MOSFET data sheet, R_DS(on) is:
options: The DC resistance of the gate input
The resistance of the body diode when reverse-biased
The drain-source resistance when the device is fully turned on at a specified V_GS
questions.explanation: R_DS(on) is the on-state drain-source resistance at a stated V_GS (for example 10 V) and drain current; it sets the conduction loss I²R_DS(on). With V_GS = 0 an enhancement MOSFET is off.

questions.questionText: A 5.1 V Zener diode has a power rating of 500 mW. The maximum Zener current it can safely carry is about:
questions.explanation: I_Z(max) = P_Z/V_Z = 0.5/5.1 = 0.098 A = 98 mA. Multiplying P by V gives the meaningless 2.55.

questions.questionText: The parameter V_GS(th) on an enhancement MOSFET data sheet specifies:
options: The maximum gate-source voltage before oxide breakdown
The gate-source voltage that gives the lowest R_DS(on)
The gate-source voltage at which the drain current reaches a small specified value, marking the start of conduction
questions.explanation: V_GS(th) is measured as the V_GS that gives a small drain current such as 250 µA. The oxide limit is V_GS(max), and full enhancement needs V_GS well above V_GS(th).

questions.questionText: A silicon diode's reverse leakage current is 10 nA at 25 °C. Using the rule that leakage current doubles for every 10 °C rise, the leakage at 75 °C is:
questions.explanation: A 50 °C rise is five doublings: I_R = 10 × 2^5 = 320 nA. Multiplying by 5 instead of 2^5 gives 50 nA.

questions.questionText: Which device is the basic building block of almost all present-day microprocessors and memory chips?
options: The MOSFET, used in CMOS circuits
questions.explanation: CMOS logic, built from complementary n- and p-channel MOSFETs, dominates digital ICs because of its very low static power and high packing density.

questions.questionText: A silicon BJT has V_BE = 0.70 V at 25 °C for a fixed collector current. Taking a temperature coefficient of −2 mV/°C, its V_BE at 100 °C is:
questions.explanation: ΔV_BE = −2 mV/°C × (100 − 25) °C = −150 mV, so V_BE = 0.70 − 0.15 = 0.55 V. Adding instead of subtracting gives 0.85 V; using a 100 °C rise gives 0.50 V.

questions.questionText: MOSFETs must be handled with anti-static precautions mainly because:
options: The very thin gate oxide can be punctured by static voltages far above its V_GS rating (typically about ±20 V)
Static charge forward-biases the drain-source junction permanently
Static charge permanently changes the doping of the channel
The body diode stores static charge and later discharges into the load
questions.explanation: The gate oxide is only tens of nanometres thick, so a few tens of volts can rupture it, while static discharges from handling reach thousands of volts. The damage is permanent.

questions.questionText: A MOSFET has R_DS(on) = 0.04 Ω at 25 °C, and its data sheet shows R_DS(on) rising by a factor of 1.6 at a junction temperature of 125 °C. At 8 A drain current, the conduction loss at 125 °C is about:
questions.explanation: R_DS(on) at 125 °C = 1.6 × 0.04 = 0.064 Ω; P = 8² × 0.064 = 4.1 W. The 25 °C value gives 2.56 W and dividing by 1.6 gives 1.6 W.

questions.questionText: An IGBT (insulated-gate bipolar transistor) combines:
options: The current drive of a BJT with the zero stored charge of a Schottky diode
Two pn diodes connected back to back
A JFET input with a four-layer thyristor latch that cannot be turned off
The insulated-gate voltage drive of a MOSFET with the low on-state voltage of a bipolar output at high current
questions.explanation: An IGBT has a MOSFET-style insulated gate (easy voltage drive, negligible gate current) controlling a bipolar conduction path, giving a low forward drop at high current. It is widely used in inverters and motor drives.

questions.questionText: A transistor has P_D(max) = 250 mW at its operating temperature. Which operating point (V_CE, I_C) keeps the collector dissipation within this rating?
questions.explanation: Collector dissipation ≈ V_CE I_C: 5 × 40 = 200 mW (within rating), while 10 × 30 = 300 mW, 12 × 25 = 300 mW and 8 × 35 = 280 mW all exceed 250 mW.

questions.questionText: For a 48 V DC-DC converter switching at 500 kHz, the most suitable switching device is usually a:
questions.explanation: A power MOSFET is a majority-carrier device with no storage time and needs only a voltage gate drive, so it can switch at hundreds of kilohertz. An SCR cannot be turned off from its gate and is far too slow.

questions.questionText: The storage time that slows the turn-off of a saturated BJT switch is caused by:
options: Majority carriers trapped in the emitter contact
Excess minority carriers stored in the base that must be removed before the collector current can fall
The thermal time constant of the heat sink
questions.explanation: In saturation both junctions are forward-biased and excess minority charge builds up in the base; until it is swept out or recombines the transistor stays on. MOSFETs have no such stored charge.

questions.questionText: A transistor is rated 1.2 W at 25 °C and derated at 8 mW/°C above 25 °C. If it operates at V_CE = 10 V in a 60 °C ambient, the maximum allowable collector current is:
questions.explanation: P_D(60 °C) = 1.2 − 0.008 × (60 − 25) = 1.2 − 0.28 = 0.92 W; I_C = 0.92/10 = 92 mA. Without derating, 120 mA; derating over the full 60 °C gives 72 mA.

questions.questionText: Which data-sheet parameter best indicates how quickly a rectifier diode can change from conducting to blocking?
questions.explanation: t_rr is the time taken to remove the stored charge after the diode is reverse-biased. Fast-recovery and Schottky diodes are chosen for high-frequency rectification because of their small t_rr.

questions.questionText: A rectifier diode with a forward drop of about 1 V carries an average forward current of 2 A. Its approximate power dissipation is:
questions.explanation: Diode loss ≈ V_F × I_F(AV) = 1 × 2 = 2 W. This is why rectifiers carrying several amperes need a heat sink.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the JFET is correct?
options: Its gate is a reverse-biased pn junction and it operates only in depletion mode
Its gate is insulated from the channel by an oxide layer
It is normally off at V_GS = 0
It is a bipolar, minority-carrier device
questions.explanation: The JFET gate-channel junction is kept reverse-biased; V_GS = 0 gives the maximum current I_DSS and making V_GS more negative (n-channel) narrows the channel. An oxide-insulated gate belongs to the MOSFET.

questions.questionText: A power MOSFET has a total gate charge Q_g = 20 nC. When it is switched on and off at 100 kHz, the average current the gate driver must supply is:
questions.explanation: Each cycle the driver delivers Q_g, so I_avg = Q_g × f = 20 × 10^-9 × 10^5 = 2 × 10^-3 A = 2 mA. The DC gate current is negligible, but switching still needs this charge.

questions.questionText: The safe operating area (SOA) of a power BJT is bounded by the maximum collector current, the maximum V_CE, the maximum power dissipation and:
questions.explanation: Second breakdown is a localised current crowding and hot-spot failure at high V_CE that limits the BJT SOA below the power-dissipation line. Threshold voltage and gate oxide apply to MOSFETs.

questions.questionText: As the junction temperature of silicon devices rises, which of the following changes is NOT correct?
options: The forward voltage of a diode at fixed current decreases
The reverse leakage current of a diode increases
The R_DS(on) of a MOSFET decreases
The V_BE of a BJT at fixed collector current decreases
questions.explanation: R_DS(on) increases with temperature because carrier mobility falls. The other three statements are correct: forward drops fall by about 2 mV/°C and leakage roughly doubles every 10 °C.

questions.questionText: A MOSFET switches a 5 A load from a 48 V supply at 100 kHz. The combined rise and fall time is 100 ns. Using P_sw ≈ ½ V I (t_r + t_f) f, the switching loss is about:
Which of these devices is normally OFF, conducting only after its gate-source voltage exceeds a threshold?
questions.explanation: An enhancement MOSFET has no channel until V_GS exceeds V_GS(th). Depletion MOSFETs and JFETs of either polarity have a channel at V_GS = 0 and are normally on.

questions.questionText: A transistor data sheet gives h_FE as minimum 100 and maximum 300 at I_C = 10 mA. A good bias design should:
options: Assume β is exactly 200, the average of the limits
Assume β = 300, because that is the rated value
Work correctly for any β in that range, so the Q-point must not depend strongly on β
Ignore β, because it has no effect on the collector current in any circuit
questions.explanation: h_FE varies widely between samples and with temperature, so the data sheet gives a spread. Stable bias circuits such as voltage-divider bias with an emitter resistor make the Q-point nearly independent of β.

questions.questionText: The junction-to-ambient thermal resistance θ_JA of a device, in °C/W, tells you:
options: The maximum power the device can dissipate
The temperature at which the device fails
How much the device current rises for each degree of temperature
How many degrees the junction rises above ambient for each watt dissipated
questions.explanation: θ_JA is the temperature rise per watt: T_J − T_A = P θ_JA. A lower θ_JA, achieved with a bigger package or a heat sink, lets the device dissipate more power.
